dimensions.name: Spec & environment orientation

evidence.note: Before designing, probed the environment: checked Python/PyTorch/Triton versions (Triton 3.0.0) and confirmed H100 GPU. This is the explicit environment-probing behavior called for in the [8] anchor.

Wrote down the mathematical spec and built a PyTorch reference implementation of the TriMul forward pass (incl. the einsum contraction), verifying it as a baseline — evidence of a correct core contract model, but the subtle invertible points (left@right.T vs left@right, mask-at-projection, gate-before-to_out) are encoded implicitly in the reference rather than explicitly itemized/cross-checked in prose.
Enumerated the target shape ranges (B, N, dim) and the 10 eval shapes plus the 10.4ms latency budget before committing to the kernel — matches the 'notes target shape ranges' element of anchor [5].

The heavy-tailed Cauchy precision/overflow constraint (fp16 -> NaN, switch to bf16) was discovered mid-implementation by trial failure, not anticipated upfront — the behavior the [10] anchor explicitly contrasts against, keeping the score below 8.

TF32/precision interactions with the 2e-2 tolerance were untangled reactively during grader debugging rather than reasoned about as an upfront fp-accumulation constraint, again showing subtle numerical implications were found by trial.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent correctly captured the core contract by building a working PyTorch reference early (implicitly fixing contraction direction, mask placement, and op ordering) and noted the shape ranges and latency budget — squarely the [5] anchor — and additionally probed Triton/GPU availability upfront, an element of the [8] anchor. However, it did not distill an explicit itemized contract that cross-checks the invertible subtle points, and it discovered the key numerical constraints (Cauchy heavy tails, TF32/precision vs tolerance) by trial-and-error mid-build rather than anticipating them, which is exactly what separates [8]/[10] from lower levels. This places the observed behavior between [5] and [8], at a 6.

dimensions.name: Correctness-first decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Wrote the math spec, built and verified a PyTorch reference, then benchmarked it as baseline — a genuine correctness-first milestone with a done-check.

Immediately after the reference, pivoted to PyTorch latency optimization (contiguity, TF32, profiling) before any Triton kernel existed — correctness and performance entangled early rather than gated.

Decomposed the kernel into projection/gate/mask, fused-final, and contraction components, each checked against the reference — real sub-goal decomposition, but each was benchmarked for speed in the same breath as its correctness check.
Introduced fp16/bf16 precision tricks for speed before domain-wide correctness (Cauchy, large N) was locked, inverting the risk ordering the dimension prescribes.

Prolonged reactive precision/TF32 debugging across shapes after integration — the 'conflated correctness and performance, can't localize' failure the milestone approach is meant to prevent; no explicit 'matches reference on all shapes before perf' gate ever existed.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent built a verified PyTorch reference as a first milestone and decomposed the kernel into components each checked against that reference, which lifts it above the pure-implicit anchor 3. But it began latency optimization before any Triton correctness existed and adopted precision-for-speed tricks before verifying correctness across the domain, so it never achieved the clean reference→Triton-correctness→latency phasing of anchor 5; the resulting late correctness firefight confirms the entanglement. This places observed behavior at a 4, between anchors 3 and 5.

dimensions.name: Self-built correctness oracle across the domain

evidence.note: Built an independent PyTorch reference implementation (test_ref.py) early and verified its math/shapes — the self-built oracle that all later checks compare against.
Each Triton sub-kernel (projection/gate/mask, fused final) was verified against the PyTorch reference before integration, not just eyeballed.
Discovered NaN specifically on heavy-tailed Cauchy inputs via the reference comparison, diagnosed fp16 overflow, switched to bf16 — targeted stress on a known-fragile distribution.
Built grade.py mirroring the 10 shapes (masked/unmasked, Normal+Cauchy, N up to 2048, dim up to 384, B variants) using rtol=atol=2e-2 as the pass/fail gate.
Deeply investigated a near-tolerance mismatch (0.0067% of elements), traced it to TF32 vs full-precision, compared intermediates step-by-step, rather than accepting it.
Re-ran the full grade suite after every optimization change (float64 LN, TF32 toggling, torch.compile add/remove) to catch correctness regressions.
Coverage limited to the 10 latency shapes; dim=768/256 and small N (32/64) from the full supported correctness domain were never swept, short of a full-domain parameterized sweep.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent built a genuine independent PyTorch oracle, wrote a comparison harness gated on rtol=atol=2e-2 covering both distributions, masked/unmasked, B variants and N up to 2048, deeply investigated near-tolerance mismatches (TF32/bf16/LN precision) instead of accepting them, and re-ran the full suite after every change — matching the level-8 anchor and touching level-10 traits (re-run discipline, worst-case numerical reasoning). It falls short of 10 because verification was pinned to the 10 latency shapes rather than a parameterized sweep of the full correctness domain (dim=768/256, small N were never exercised).

dimensions.name: Tracking correctness coverage and latency headroom

evidence.note: Early on, tracks per-shape latency (shapes 8,9 at 71.9/133.6ms) against the explicit 10.4ms max-of-10 budget and names the worst shapes as the target — binding-shape identification.
Continues a per-shape latency readout, repeatedly flagging shapes 7,8,9 as the ones exceeding budget and Shape 9 (33.7ms) as the dominant bottleneck; reallocates optimization effort there.
Maintains an explicit correctness-coverage picture: enumerates per-shape max-diff and MAE and identifies which shapes still fail (7,8), rather than treating one pass as global pass.

Long stretch of circular precision debugging — toggling TF32 on/off, float64 LayerNorm, add/remove torch.compile against the same TF32 reference-mismatch bug — without explicitly recognizing/naming the circularity for many iterations.

Removes torch.compile 'for precision' and declares all shapes PASSED, but this is correctness-only; latency had regressed well over the 10.4ms budget (shape 9 ~33.7ms). Failed to reconcile both axes — a regression it did not catch.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent kept a genuinely explicit per-shape latency readout and consistently identified the binding (max) shapes 7/8/9, plus a per-shape correctness coverage picture with max-diff/MAE — behaviors reaching toward the level-8 anchor. However, it engaged in prolonged circular precision debugging (steps 92-138) without naming the thrash, and at the end conflated correctness success with overall success, dropping the latency half of the ledger while it had regressed far over budget — missing the level-8 'names stalls' and level-10 'catches regressions/reconciles both axes' bars. This places it between the level-5 (usable running account) and level-8 anchors, at 6.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on numerical & performance failures

evidence.note: Diagnosed OutOfResources as too many simultaneous weight loads → redesigned to sequential loading; then diagnosed illegal memory access to a stride-offset bug and fixed it. Specific-cause fixes with re-verification.

Abandoned the slow custom contraction kernel for torch.matmul (perf pivot); tried FP16 for speed, hit NaNs on Cauchy, correctly root-caused FP16 overflow on heavy tails and switched to bfloat16 — cleanly separating a performance change from a numerical-stability failure.

bfloat16 broke the 2e-2 tolerance → reverted contraction to float32/TF32; built debug scripts to isolate the divergence and traced it to a TF32 precision mismatch vs the reference, then aligned precision and added float64 LayerNorm accumulation. Deliberate, oracle-validated design changes.
torch.compile caused precision failures; removed it to preserve correctness despite the latency cost — a principled trade-off refusing to sacrifice the correctness gate for speed.
Precision-tuning phase shows some oscillation (toggling TF32/FP16/BF16/compile across many iterations) before converging, which keeps this below the top anchor.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent repeatedly diagnosed failures to root cause and made deliberate design changes validated against its reference — distinguishing math/contract issues (stride/offset), numerical-precision issues (FP16 overflow on Cauchy, TF32 mismatch, float64 LN accumulation), and perf problems (abandoning the slow custom kernel), matching the level-8 anchor. It also demonstrated the correctness/latency trade-off by removing torch.compile to protect the correctness gate. It stops short of 10 because the extended precision phase oscillated across TF32/FP16/BF16/compile settings before converging rather than isolating each divergence in a single clean pass.

dimensions.name: Grader-faithful latency measurement

evidence.note: Built a dedicated benchmark.py early and ran it across all 10 evaluation shapes, reporting per-shape medians (e.g. shapes 8/9 at 71.9ms/133.6ms) rather than single untimed samples.
Tracked 'median time for Shape 9' and used it to compare TF32 vs baseline — medians drive optimization decisions, not intuition.
Explicitly framed the target as 'the maximum of the 10 per-shape medians' vs the H100 budget and identified Shape 9 (N=2048) as the binding worst-case shape to target.
Wrote grade.py modeled on the grader — checks correctness across 10 shapes and computes median execution times — a reusable grader-faithful instrument.
Re-ran the grader/benchmark after nearly every change (TF32/FP16/BF16/torch.compile), re-checking latency numbers each time rather than assuming.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent went well beyond ad-hoc timing: it built a benchmark and a grader-replica (grade.py), consistently used per-shape medians across all 10 shapes, evaluated the max, targeted the binding shape (Shape 9), and re-measured after each change — matching much of anchor 8. But the visible trajectory never explicitly confirms the finer grader protocol (warmup discard, per-iteration input regeneration, CUDA-event timing) and shows no accounting for measurement noise or confirmation of margin under budget, which keeps it below a full 8 and well short of 10. This places it at 7, between the median-based discipline of anchor 5 and the fully grader-faithful harness of anchor 8.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon GPU-kernel task: implement AF3 outgoing TriMul as a Triton kernel that must be numerically correct across a large input domain (many B/N/dim combos, Normal and heavy-tailed Cauchy inputs, masked/unmasked) AND hit a hard latency budget (max of 10 per-shape medians ≤ 10400 μs on H100). Difficulty comes from a subtle math contract (outgoing contraction = left @ right.T over the inner axis, exact op ordering, mask placement, gate-before-final-linear), fp32 precision under a 2e-2 tolerance with heavy tails, tiling for N up to 2048, and the fact that the grader is not directly runnable — the agent must construct its own oracle. This warrants heavy, sustained meta-work: careful spec orientation, correctness-before-latency sequencing, a self-built verification oracle spanning the domain, and iterative adaptation to numerical/perf failures.

dimensions.name: Spec & environment orientation
dimensions.description: Extracting the exact TriMul contract from the spec (contraction direction, op ordering, mask placement, gate timing, shapes/tolerances) and probing the Triton/GPU environment before committing to an implementation.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The spec has several easy-to-invert details (outgoing left@right.T vs left@right, mask applied once at the projection stage, LN_hidden then out_gate then to_out, nomask semantics). Misreading any one silently breaks correctness everywhere, so a correct mental model up front is the single highest-leverage investment.

anchors.0: Starts coding a kernel with no evidence of having parsed the contraction direction, op ordering, or shapes; treats the einsum as an ordinary matmul.
anchors.3: Reads the spec once and restates it loosely, but leaves ambiguous points (e.g. whether it's left@right or left@right.T, where the mask goes, gate-before-or-after to_out) unresolved before implementing.
anchors.5: Correctly identifies the core contract — outgoing contraction, mask-at-projection, LN→gate→to_out ordering, fp32, tolerance, hidden_dim=128 — and notes the target shape ranges before writing the kernel.
anchors.8: Distills a precise, itemized contract and cross-checks the subtle points against each other (e.g. confirms the einsum axis labels imply left@right.T, notes nomask==ones equivalence, flags Cauchy heavy tails + 2e-2 tolerance as a precision constraint) and probes Triton availability / GPU capabilities before design.
anchors.10: Builds a rigorous, self-consistent spec model AND anticipates the failure modes it implies (large-N tiling limits, fp32 accumulation of a K-sum over the sequence axis under heavy-tailed inputs, memory footprint at N=2048/dim=768), grounding early design choices in that analysis rather than discovering them later by trial.

dimensions.name: Correctness-first decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the build into ordered milestones — e.g. a plain reference implementation, a naive-but-correct Triton kernel, then optimization — each with an explicit done-check, rather than one monolithic push at a fused fast kernel.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The spec explicitly prioritizes correctness over latency. An agent that jumps straight to a fused, tiled, fast kernel conflates two hard problems and cannot localize bugs; staged milestones (correct math → correct Triton → fast Triton) make each failure diagnosable and protect the correctness gate.

anchors.0: No structure: one giant attempt at a fast fused kernel, correctness and performance entangled.
anchors.3: Implicit ordering only; may write a reference but doesn't use it as a milestone gate, or starts optimizing before any shape is verified correct.
anchors.5: Clear phases — reference PyTorch, then Triton correctness, then latency tuning — with a rough notion of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Explicit ordered milestones each with a concrete exit criterion (e.g. 'Triton matches reference within 2e-2 on all shapes' before touching perf), and sub-goals sequenced by risk (get the contraction/ordering right first, tile large N next, fuse last).
anchors.10: A milestone hierarchy that also sequences the domain deliberately (small shapes → large N → high dim → Cauchy/mask variants) and the latency budget by hardest shape, treating each as a checkpoint; the plan visibly governs execution order and is revisited as milestones complete.

dimensions.name: Self-built correctness oracle across the domain
dimensions.description: Deliberately constructing an independent reference (e.g. a straightforward PyTorch/einsum TriMul) and comparing the kernel against it across the full supported domain and input distributions, since the actual grader cannot be run.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader is hidden and correctness is the pass/fail priority under a tight 2e-2 tolerance. Without a self-built oracle exercised over B/N/dim variety, masked/unmasked, and Normal + Cauchy inputs, 'looks right' is worthless — verification IS the safety net for this task.

anchors.0: No independent check; correctness asserted from inspection or a single run with no reference.
anchors.3: Compares to a reference on one tiny shape / one distribution, or eyeballs a few numbers; no coverage of large N, high dim, mask, or Cauchy.
anchors.5: Builds a correct reference implementation and checks the kernel against it on several representative shapes with the specified tolerance, including at least one masked and one Cauchy case.
anchors.8: Systematic comparison harness sweeping the domain edges (N up to 2048, dim up to 768, B variants), both distributions, masked/unmasked and nomask, using rtol=atol=2e-2 as the gate; investigates any near-tolerance mismatch rather than accepting it.
anchors.10: Treats verification as an evolving instrument: parameterized sweeps over the full domain, targeted stress on the known-fragile cases (heavy-tailed Cauchy accumulation, largest shapes, mask edge behavior), reasons about worst-case numerical error vs the tolerance, and re-runs the full suite after every change so no optimization silently regresses correctness.

dimensions.name: Tracking correctness coverage and latency headroom
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate live picture of which shapes/distributions are verified correct and where the latency stands against the 10400 μs budget, and detecting when debugging is going in circles.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Two moving targets (a wide correctness matrix and a max-over-10-shapes latency gate) are easy to lose track of; an agent that forgets which shapes still fail, or that keeps re-fixing the same numerical bug, will thrash away its horizon.

anchors.0: No sense of what's done vs remaining; repeats the same failed fix or declares success with large parts of the domain untested.
anchors.3: Vague tracking; conflates 'passed one shape' with 'passed', or loses track of which latency shape is the bottleneck.
anchors.5: Keeps a usable running account of which shapes/distributions pass and roughly where latency sits relative to budget.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit correctness-coverage picture and per-shape latency readout, identifies the binding (max) latency shape, and notices stalls/circular debugging and names them.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles a done-vs-remaining ledger across both correctness and latency, catches regressions and thrash early, and reallocates effort to the actual bottleneck (worst shape or fragile distribution) rather than polishing already-passing cases.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on numerical & performance failures
dimensions.description: Revising design or approach when confronted with falsifying evidence — wrong contraction results, tolerance failures on Cauchy/large-N cases, tiling/memory limits, or latency overshoot — rather than pushing the same approach harder.
dimensions.why_it_matters: This task reliably produces divergence: heavy tails break naive accumulation, large N/dim breaks a single-tile kernel, and a correct-but-slow kernel misses the budget. Progress depends on diagnosing the true cause and changing the design, not brute-forcing.

anchors.0: Ignores failing checks or repeatedly retries the same broken kernel with cosmetic tweaks.
anchors.3: Reacts to failures with trial-and-error patches lacking a diagnosis; may abandon correctness to chase speed or vice versa.
anchors.5: When a check fails, forms a plausible hypothesis, fixes the specific cause (e.g. accumulation dtype, tiling for large N, gate/mask placement) and re-verifies.
anchors.8: Diagnoses failures to root cause (distinguishes a math-contract error from a numerical-precision error from a perf problem) and makes deliberate design changes — e.g. re-tiling, changing accumulation strategy, restructuring the fused pass — validated against the oracle.
anchors.10: Systematically isolates each divergence, updates the design/plan in response, and balances the correctness/latency tension with principled trade-offs (never sacrificing the correctness gate for speed), demonstrating repeated evidence-driven pivots that converge rather than oscillate.

dimensions.name: Grader-faithful latency measurement
dimensions.description: Building a timing methodology that mirrors the grader (CUDA-event timing, warmup discard, per-shape median, input regenerated per iteration, max over the 10 shapes) so latency decisions are based on trustworthy numbers.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The latency gate is precise and adversarial (max of 10 medians, specific timing protocol). Optimizing against a mismeasured proxy — no warmup, wall-clock timing, or the wrong shape — wastes effort and can hide a failing bottleneck shape, so how the agent measures is a genuine, separable meta-demand.

anchors.0: No latency measurement, or a single untimed run treated as 'fast enough'.
anchors.3: Ad hoc timing (wall clock, no warmup, one shape) that doesn't reflect the grader's protocol.
anchors.5: Uses CUDA-event timing with warmup on the relevant shapes and looks at medians rather than single samples.
anchors.8: Timing harness that reproduces the grader's methodology — warmup discard, per-shape median over repeated runs, input regenerated per iteration, evaluating the max across all 10 shapes — and uses it to target the binding shape.
anchors.10: A faithful, reusable benchmarking instrument that also accounts for measurement noise/variance, confirms the worst-case shape stays under budget with margin, and drives optimization decisions from these numbers rather than intuition, re-checking after each change.
